messages:
andrea: FYI ran a broad perf sweep for the mixed FP8/INT4 kernels with our continuous batcher today. found a sharp throughput cliff for mid-sized batches + long seqs.

samir: can you paste the raw numbers and the hardware details?

andrea: A100v4, driver 535.xx, nightly runtime. short summary: fp8-fast-path underperforms int4-fallback for certain (batch, seq, kv-align) combos. snippet below.

andrea: ```
# tokens/sec (sample shapes)
bs=4 seq=512 align=128 -> fp8: 46k, int4: 63k
bs=6 seq=512 align=128 -> fp8: 44k, int4: 60k
bs=4 seq=128 align=128 -> fp8: 88k, int4: 81k
bs=8 seq=64  align=64  -> fp8: 120k, int4: 118k
```

mika: odd that fp8 loses to int4 at 512. did you capture SM occupancy and shared-mem usage?

andrea: yes, added microprofile: fp8 kernel drops shared_mem efficiency when tile shapes cross a 48KB boundary in our codegen. occupancy falls ~20%. int4 path uses different tile tiling and keeps occupancy.

kai: what about KV cache behavior? continuous batching can pack many small prefixes into a single request; that can create fragmentation and extra memcpy.

andrea: KV profiler shows ~30% of requests get split into multiple slabs due to per-layer stripe alignment -> avg extra memcpy ~1.6ms/request, variance high. when that extra cost lines up with the fp8 slow-path it amplifies throughput loss.

samir: that memcpy is huge relative to per-token work at these seq lengths. two hypotheses: (1) kernel tiling crosses sub-block boundaries causing poor CIL lanes, (2) KV slot alignment/allocator causing extra memcpy and misaligned loads.

mika: do we have a quick sim for changing slot alignment and seeing perf?

andrea: ran a sim toggling alignment 128->256. results: for the problematic shapes fp8 improved ~15% with align=256; but short-seq shapes saw regression ~6%. so no single global alignment sweeps all shapes.

kai: sounds like we need per-route or per-seq-dist heuristics: selector should consider batch, seq-dist percentiles, kv-frag rate, and pick kernel+alignment combo.

andrea: agreed. also noticed calibration affects codegen: slight shift in quant scales causes the fp8 path to pick a different shared-mem layout (fast vs fallback). so calibration impacts latency/throughput, not just accuracy.

samir: meaning our calibration pipeline must include perf as an objective. quality-only calibration will push some workloads onto the slow path.

mika: propose a compact cost model in the selector: inputs {bs, p50_seq, p95_seq, kv_frag_rate, alignment} -> predicts tokens/sec and p99 tail. cheap linear model or small XGBoost trained from microbench grid.

kai: low-risk rollout: offline sampling per-route (we already sample ~1k reqs), fit the cost model, then the selector uses it to pick kernel+alignment. we can A/B test on dedicated clusters.

andrea: I'll prototype a simple linear-reg baseline that runs in-selector. experiment harness will output a CSV of predicted vs measured.

samir: also add telemetry: when selector chooses fp8 but actual perf is worse than predicted, emit a sampling trace so we can retrain.

mika: for on-prem/private customers include an opt-out flag for alignment tuning. do not mutate deployed alignment without explicit consent.

andrea: action items: 1) andrea: add selector cost-model + alignment tuning flags, push branch + PR (ETA 2d). 2) samir: run full microbench across shape grid and collect occupancy/SM-eff metrics (ETA 1d). 3) kai: build per-route sample->calibration->perf CSV pipeline (ETA 3d).

andrea: one more gotcha: padding-waste calc in cost model must weight by token-distribution tail (p95/p99), not just mean seq. otherwise kernel picks favoring mean cause high tail-waste for long sequences.

kai: +1. use histogram-weighted expected tokens and penalty term for p99.

infra-bot: perf artifacts uploaded: s3://redwood-perf/1758460011/run_archive.tar.gz 

samir: perfect. once we have the csvs I'll run a quick canary on dedicated cluster and compare latency/cost.

andrea: will post the PR and perf plots here when ready. thanks all.

kai: great progress, seems like a realistic route to reduce tail and lower unit-cost. :rocket:
